entries.title: Spain in the Balance
entries.summary: This past summer was Spain’s hottest on record. In Valencia, where I spent August, a series of ongoing heat waves regularly pushed the daily temperature past 97 degrees Fahrenheit. entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
This past summer was Spain’s hottest on record. In Valencia, where I spent August, a series of ongoing heat waves regularly pushed the daily temperature past 97 degrees Fahrenheit. On most days it was too hot to be outside between 11 AM and 7 PM, and the muggy evening air offered little respite. Fires ravaged rural areas to the west and north, and caused the evacuation of villages near Madrid. Millions of trees burned. On my last night I was watching TV with the windows open when I noticed a carcinogenic smell. The sky outside was the color of ash, settling over a parched landscape. A fire had broken out in El Saler, a nature preserve and beach more than twenty miles away, and winds had carried the smoke inland.

It was a summer of crises for Spain, where a snap election on November 29 will determine whether the nation remains under one of Europe’s only left-wing coalition governments or succumbs to the rising right. Many of the European Union’s longstanding sources of tension—climate change, immigration, housing—have collided here with particular force. Like Italy, Greece, and other countries in southern Europe, Spain faces more urgent climate stresses than its northern neighbors. Some 74 percent of the country’s territory is at risk of desertification, while flash floods have devastated Valencia and water supply shortages continue to affect Catalonia. The 2024 floods killed 230 people; in the past three years more than 11,000 have died from excess heat.

Immigration has meanwhile become a central rift in the country’s politics. The majority of Spaniards support legal pathways for residency, but 72 percent oppose irregular migration. The ascendant far-right party Vox goes further, calling for “remigration” and adopting the campaign slogan “Ni uno más” (“not one more”).

This summer the issue became a political maelstrom. The catalyst was migration from Ceuta, a Spanish city on Africa’s northern coast that borders Morocco and faces the Strait of Gibraltar. (Ceuta itself was “given” to Spain by Portugal during the height of European colonialism in 1668.) In late July some 70,000 North African migrants, most of them Moroccan, crossed from Morocco to Ceuta over the course of two days. Many swam along the coast to avoid being stopped by immigration officers; nearly 150 people drowned. As European Union President Ursula von der Leyen panicked about the new arrivals, demanding even more militarized borders, Vox’s leader, Santiago Abascal, predictably issued a dog whistle, calling it “an invasion.” The episode prompted a surge of racist media coverage and online hate speech directed toward migrants.

Then, as September began, a housing crisis long in the making erupted. It was not a surprise. I had been coming to Valencia from Berlin regularly over the past three years, and I knew that much was changing in what had once been a relatively relaxed coastal city, where painters could still afford studios and the average almuerzo—the local meal between breakfast and lunch, characterized by a giant bocadillo, a coffee, and copious plates of peanuts and olives—cost six euros. Spanish friends in Valencia had been increasingly displaced as landlords drastically increased rental costs; the average rent has doubled in the last five years. In Madrid, which has always been one of Spain’s most expensive cities, rents have also skyrocketed, now exceeding 70 percent of the average worker’s salary. Across the country, the average person paid at least 50 percent of their income toward housing in 2025.

On September 23 police evicted an eighty-seven-year-old woman named Maricarmen Abascal (no relation to the Vox leader) from the Madrid apartment her family had rented for seven decades. Maricarmen, as she was widely known, resided in the central Retiro neighborhood, where she had long paid around €500 for her rent-controlled flat and utilities, living on her €1,350-a-month pension, the average social security stipend. Six years ago a Madrid real estate firm named Urbagestión purchased her building, set the new rent at €2,650, and claimed that Maricarmen’s lease was invalid because it had been passed from her father to her mother and then to her. (Under Franco-era laws, the wife could not be listed on the original contract.) As the case became a cause célèbre, the company seemed set on garnering ill will, turning down offers from an anonymous writer who wanted to pay the rental difference for the rest of Maricarmen’s life and from Spain’s housing minister, who tried to purchase the apartment.

Protestors, many of them students, camped out in Madrid’s Puerta del Sol square for weeks in anticipation of an eviction, ultimately numbering some one thousand people. By the morning of September 23 the state had attempted three times to evict Maricarmen and failed due to legal appeals and public pressure. This time they persisted. Images of riot-uniformed officers breaking into her apartment and then paramedics carrying her out on a stretcher ricocheted around the world; in Spain they galvanized a wave of new demonstrations in Barcelona, Valencia, Palma, and Cáceres. A few days later Urbagestión relented and offered to let Maricarmen resume the lease for an undisclosed figure close to her previous rent, but it was too late; she died on October 7 in Madrid’s Gregorio Marañón Hospital before she could return home. In her last public statement she said: “keep fighting for what is yours.”

Advertisement

These overlapping social ruptures have put Spain’s long-serving prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, in a particularly difficult position. Since the Madrid-born economist improbably became the country’s leader in 2018, when his Socialist Party (PSOE) held only eighty-four of the 350 seats in Congress, he has weathered multiple crises within both the nation’s fractured political system and the country at large. Spaniards often sum up his skill at getting out of political trouble with the saying “tener una flor en el culo”—“you have a flower in your ass.”

Outside of Spain, Sánchez has emerged as a progressive icon over the past two years. In May 2025 he declared in parliament that Israel was a “genocidal state,” and a month later he called for the EU to suspend ties with the country. He was quick to push back against the US–Israeli war on Iran, denying the Americans use of their military bases on Spanish territory for armed conflict. This past September he met New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly for a morning breakfast event, “Building an Economy for the Many.”

Inside Spain, however, Sánchez is seen less as a leftist firebrand than as an Obama-esque centrist defined by his pragmatism and charm. He is extraordinarily skilled at dealing with the media, often turning his opponents’ insults to his advantage. When the right began calling him “Perro Sánchez” or “Perro Sanxe” (Sánchez the Dog) years ago, he and his political team reclaimed the image—most recently in late October, when Sánchez appeared on the talk show La Revuelta and gifted the host David Broncano a dog-shaped cookie jar. When he published an autobiography in 2019, he called it A Manual of Resistance.

These tactics, however, have not been enough to overcome the fact that Sánchez has faced especially difficult political headwinds in recent years. In snap general elections in 2023 the PSOE came in second behind its main opponent, the center-right People’s Party (PP). Sánchez managed to form a new governing coalition and gain a third term, but the PP controlled the Senate, and Sánchez’s majority grew more unstable as it expanded to include smaller forces, notably the Catalan pro-independence party Junts. Since then Sánchez has struggled to pass ambitious legislation or even a functioning budget, facing opposition from the right (the PP and Vox), the Catalan separatists (primarily Junts), and the left (primarily Podemos, the anti-austerity party founded in 2014).

In recent months Sánchez has attempted to play his political cards as best he can. This summer he visited the fire-damaged areas, called for a national political agreement on climate, and launched a national climate-shelter network. As the Ceuta crisis erupted, he tried to strike a balance between taking a humane tone—praising border guards who had let people through as opposed to causing more deaths—and swiftly facilitating mass returns, even as EU heads of state blamed the incident, without evidence, on his decision earlier in the year to allow undocumented migrants a pathway to regularize their status.

Lately he has staked his tenure on housing rights. Amid the Maricarmen protests, Sánchez proposed nationwide reforms to suspend evictions until 2030 and constrain rent increases, but the changes were predictably blocked in parliament by the PP, along with Vox and Junts. Three days later Sánchez called a snap parliamentary election. “You must decide,” he declared to the nation at large, “whether you want our country to move backwards or continue moving forwards, and whether you prefer a government that works for the interests of the majority of society.” Three-hundred and fifty seats in the Congress of Deputies are up for election on November 29, as well as 209 of 267 seats in the Senate. Whichever party receives the most votes will try to form a government; Congress will then vote on the prime minister.

Previously a nationwide election had been scheduled for next summer; Sánchez likely hoped to capitalize on the swell of public anger over housing to rally left-leaning voters. His opinion polls had been low for months. It could have been another flor en el culo moment, but in late October a high-speed train crash—the second of the year—killed sixty-nine people and shifted the national conversation at least temporarily from housing rights to administrative failures. For weeks the PP led predictions, though as of November 15 most polls showed an almost dead heat between them and the PSOE.

Advertisement

Should the PSOE win, Sánchez’s only chance at maintaining his coalition would be to forge alliances with leftist parties that have often criticized him, including Podemos, Frente Amplio (previously Sumar, a coalition of four parties with which he is currently in government), and three left-wing Catalan, Basque, and Galician parties: the ERC (Esquerra Republicana de Catalunya), EH Bildu (Euskal Herria Bildu), and the BNG (Galician Nationalist Bloc). He would also likely need the Catalan and Basque center-right parties, despite the fact that Junts recently killed his housing reforms. It’s unclear if even this fragmented coalition would provide Sánchez with the majority he needs to form a government: as of now Vox is polling at 19.8 percent, much higher than any of the leftist parties.

If the PP wins, they have indicated that they will likely form a governing coalition with Vox, whose leaders openly yearn for the return of a Christian country that rejects regional autonomy, restricts human rights, and promotes the heteronormative nuclear family. It would be the first time since Franco’s death in 1975 that the nationalist right regained power. In this sense the outcome of the election is existential not just for Sánchez but for the nation.

Sánchez is a long-term member of the PSOE, the historically working-class party founded in Madrid in 1879. Having first joined as a student, he served on the Madrid city council and in Congress, alternating between public service and academia, where he was an economics lecturer. Sánchez was virtually unknown nationally when he made a successful bid for party leadership in the PSOE primaries in 2014; his outsider status became part of his political identity. Today the PSOE is socially progressive and pro-EU. Fiscally it supports social-democratic policies that seek to alleviate inequality without radically overhauling the market-based system.

To its left are a variety of parties that would like to see more progressive measures. Podemos and Frente Amplio (formerly Sumar), for example, advocate for more aggressive taxes on the wealthy and corporations. On foreign policy, the PSOE commits to continued NATO membership, while Podemos and more recently Frente Amplio would like to see Spain withdraw; the PSOE has also gradually sided with Morocco over autonomy for Western Sahara, the territory that the North African country has occupied since Franco’s Spain withdrew from its former colony in 1975, while Podemos, Frente Amplio, and the ERC support independence for the region’s Sahrawi people. Then there are the smaller parties, like the ERC, that support Catalan, Galician, and Basque self-determination, which often puts them at odd with the PSOE’s vision of a united Spain. These are just a few of the policy differences dividing the left, which has also struggled with heated leadership rivalries. “More egos than seats” read a recent editorial in El Diaro from the commentator Lucía Taboada.

From the beginning of his national political career, Sánchez has been willing to forge unusual alliances, including with the right, rather than compromise with the left. In 2016 talks with Podemos broke down, in part because Sánchez simultaneously pursued a policy agreement with the center-right Ciudadanos. After an election in April 2019, when the PSOE won 28.7 percent of the vote and Podemos and its regional allies received some 14.3 percent, the two parties again failed to reach a pact to form a leftist government: negotiations collapsed primarily over cabinet posts and power-sharing. (They eventually reached an agreement later in the year, after another election; the arrangement lasted until 2023, when the PSOE instead entered into coalition with Sumar.) The ERC’s Gabriel Rufián, who represents Barcelona in Congress, criticized both parties at the time for failing to make the needed concessions. “The left has lost its entire existence while the right smiles,” he argued.

Sánchez has also been willing to break campaign promises to stay in power. In 2024 he backed a law that exonerated those involved in Catalonia’s 2017 separatist referendum, reversing a previous position against amnesty for Catalan separatists. The deal secured him the support he needed from Junts and the ERC to remain Spain’s leader, but it also triggered mass protests.

Over the past four years Sánchez has raised the minimum wage, strengthened unemployment protections, extended paid parental leave, passed some tenant protections, restored access to abortion for sixteen- and seventeen-year-olds without parental consent, created legal gender recognition based on self-determination, and provided pathways for 600,000 undocumented migrants to achieve legal status. And yet he has not resolved some of the central problems polarizing the nation—including the fact that many people cannot afford basic goods even as business in the country booms. In 2025 Spain’s economy grew by 2.8 percent, according to an IMF estimate, outperforming Germany and other wealthy countries. Real GDP per person, on the other hand, grew by only 1.8 percent. Combined with a housing affordability crisis and rising grocery prices—Spain has the second-highest food inflation in Europe—the average person finds it increasingly hard to keep the lights on.

Many of Sánchez’s more ambitious proposals to address this problem have been blocked in Congress by Vox, the PP, and Junts. But if the right has obstructed Sánchez from alleviating the country’s economic plight, it has also wasted few opportunities to capitalize on the resulting discontent. Vox has blamed rising rent and grocery prices on government intervention, taxation, and immigration. Their recent election campaign, “inalquilable” (“unrentable”), features renters unable to navigate the housing market.

The left has fought to reclaim the issue. Last week the country’s two largest labor unions, the General Union of Workers (UGT) and the Workers’ Commissions (CCOO), organized the first general strike in fourteen years as a protest over the housing crisis. For one day, Spain ground to a halt. Afterwards Sánchez’s housing reforms finally passed Congress, but the PP has already stated that it will repeal them if it wins the election.

Another problem plaguing Sánchez has been a steady drip of corruption charges implicating PSOE officials. The Spanish Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office has brought criminal charges against several prominent PSOE figures; in June Sánchez’s former Transport Minister José Luis Ábalos was sentenced to twenty-four years and three months in prison for receiving kickbacks on sales of personal protective equipment during the Covid-19 pandemic. Sánchez swiftly condemned Ábalos’s actions, claiming he had no knowledge of them.

Allegations of financial impropriety and “influence peddling” have also been levied against Sánchez’s own family members, including his wife, Begoña Gómez. In Spain a constitutional article called the “popular prosecution” allows a citizen or group to bring criminal charges, and in Gómez’s case a coalition of far-right groups—including Vox—has done precisely that, accusing her of using her position as Sánchez’s wife to obtain a post at a Madrid university and then allocating public funds to a software project. Although a Spanish prosecutor asked the judge, Juan Carlos ​Peinado, to drop the case, Peinado ordered Gomez to stand trial in the coming months and banned her from leaving the country. Sánchez has consistently defended Gómez, calling the charges politically motivated and at one point threatening to resign over the persecution of his family. (Charges were also brought against his brother David by the same organization for receiving a regional position overseeing public music schools; he was acquitted of influence peddling but convicted of “administrative misconduct,” a ruling he is currently appealing.)

Corruption in Spanish politics is not limited to the PSOE. Prior to Sánchez’s tenure, the PP-led government collapsed in 2018 after an enormous scandal called Caso Gürtel triggered a vote of no confidence against the prime minister at the time, Mariano Rajoy. Caso Gürtel, also occasionally called “the Spanish Watergate,” involved dozens of officials who received bribes for public contracts, including Luis Bárcenas, the former PP national treasurer, who was convicted of receiving €1.24 million. (The PP was also convicted as a civil beneficiary of the scheme.) In Transparency International’s 2025 Corruption Perceptions Index, Spain scored only 55 out of 100, and the country has even experimented with running rehab programs for crooked administrators. Nonetheless, Sánchez campaigned originally on an anti-corruption platform; the accusations and charges have damaged his ability to lead.

The PP, headed by the prime ministerial candidate Alberto Núñez Feijóo, offers a radically different vision than Sánchez’s. On November 10 the party issued a 249-point electoral manifesto that promised to largely undo many of Sánchez’s reforms and achievements over the past eight years. They would build one million new homes (rather than regulate landlords), introduce tax cuts, increase migrant deportations, introduce stricter welfare requirements, and repeal several high-profile laws. Among them is the Law of Democratic Memory, passed four years ago, which established an official Register of Victims from the years of the dictatorship, mandated the removal of Francoist symbols, and restored citizenship for the descendants of Spaniards who were exiled or forced to flee the country to save their lives. The PP officially recognizes that Franco was a dictator, but in 2021 their then-leader argued that the law would merely be a way to “dig up grudges,” a position they continue to hold.

Sánchez is right that Spain, like most former colonial European countries, has always been caught between its past and its future. Undercurrents of nostalgia for the dictatorship have ebbed and flowed over the past four decades. Today 20 percent of Spanish people continue to view Franco’s regime positively, part of a broader romanticization of fascism that has rebounded across the continent: last year a social media campaign called “Life was better under Franco” trended on TikTok.

That the historical amnesia about Franco’s cruelties has made it into both the PP’s and Vox’s policies is not surprising in a country that adopted a Pacto del Olvido (“Pact of Forgetting”) to swiftly transition to democracy without ever holding anyone accountable for the dictatorship. Even after the passage of the Law of Democratic Memory, no official has been convicted for crimes committed under Franco’s leadership, which range from torture to enforced disappearances to extrajudicial executions. Unmarked mass graves contain the bones of tens of thousands of civil war victims, while more than a hundred survivors of torture continue to seek justice.

The forces holding back Spain’s tide of resurgent right-wing politics are in some respects as embattled and divided now as they have ever been. Earlier this year the ERC’s Gabriel Rufián called for the creation of a new alliance to keep the far right from power. His proposal never advanced, shot down in part by the head of his own party. When other leftist groups—including Izquierda Unida (United Left), Movimiento Sumar, Más Madrid, and Comuns—decided to form the Frente Amplio coalition, negotiations with Podemos failed over candidate lists. Now that a tight election looms, these divisions could be especially costly. “Si no nos unimos, nos matarán por separado,” Rufián has said multiple times to the country: “If we don’t unite, they will kill us one by one.”

entries.title: Celia Paul on Her Memoir, Life, and Art
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
In this episode of Private Life, Celia Paul joins Jarrett Earnest for a conversation about her art, writing, and life. Paul reflects on self-portraiture, grief, her relationship with Lucien Freud, and the painting La Tempesta by Giorgione, which figures prominently in her new memoir, Objects of Desire: An Artist in Venice, published this month by New York Review Books.  

Celia Paul is a British painter based in London. She studied at the Slade School of Fine Art from 1976 to 1981. Her work is in the collections of the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the British Museum, and the National Portrait Gallery in London. Gladstone Gallery presented a solo exhibition of Paul’s work titled Innervisions in the spring of 2026. A solo show, Celia Paul: Objects of Desire, is now open at Victoria Miro Venice. She is also the author of Self Portrait (2020) and Letters to Gwen John (2022), both published by NYRB.

You can find Objects of Desire and other books by Celia Paul at nyrb.com or at your favorite bookseller.

entries.title: The Struggle Has Begun
entries.summary: With so many horrors to choose from—the lies and broken promises; the violence, sadism, and vengefulness; the extortion, graft, and grift; the open contempt for the laws, stated ideals, and noncriminal residents of the country that the current administration was elected to steward—an exasperated public had no need to wrack its brains over what issues […]
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
With so many horrors to choose from—the lies and broken promises; the violence, sadism, and vengefulness; the extortion, graft, and grift; the open contempt for the laws, stated ideals, and noncriminal residents of the country that the current administration was elected to steward—an exasperated public had no need to wrack its brains over what issues to vote on, and simply returned a resounding Enough.

As the results came in, the great national exhalation expressed the relief of a dreamer when the parachute finally opens after all. But the dream itself senses the alligator swamp below, and stretching beyond it burned bridges, sacked storehouses, gutted libraries, bombed-out schools, and fields piled high with corpses. The interregnum between now and January promises months of held breath.

One area of concern, obviously, is our fanciful president. How much damage will he effect before, cornered and raging, he can be hauled off the main stage? And how much of that damage will be intentional, and how much accidental—a cigarette butt casually dropped into a dry forest? A second worry is the thugs the president is splashing around into ever more prominent positions, most threateningly the spectacularly vile Stephen Miller as chief of staff, and most comically (or maybe most depressingly) the mixed-martial-arts impresario Dana White, who declined Trump’s half-hearted invitation to serve as press secretary. A third concern are the sinister “intellectuals” of the MAGA movement—the authors, for instance of Project 2025, the shadowy white supremacist jurists, “educators,” and tactics geeks. They are dogged, crafty, and resourceful, and they endure.

But those concerns are specific to the Republican Party—and not all of it, at that. If January comes without some new, astoundingly irrational and destructive foreign adventure, or new legislation that’s a death knell to the environment, or a new ghoul seated on the Supreme Court, or a total economic collapse, it will be the Democratic Party and individual Democratic lawmakers who are floodlit as the serious, the true engines of anxiety production. The question is already everywhere: Will the Democrats seize the opportunity—no, the mandate!—they’ve been given, to create from the wreckage a model for a working society in the form of a constitutional democracy, or will they simply modify the cruel policies of the Trump years and return to a lethal status quo? The struggle has begun, as evidenced in flurries of emails, endless articles, calls for meetings, chatter everywhere, and, concretely, in the sudden, unexpected possibility of Chuck Schumer being replaced in January as the Senate majority leader by Chris Van Hollen.

Voters were polled right after voting day. Polling questions are broad approximations, and respondents say what they say, but results probably yield some information. Large numbers said they voted Democrat because of “the cost of living.” And few would argue that increased and unpredictable expenses have been a trivial concern. But a more revealing reason cited by a very large number of voters was “corruption.”

The word cannot be shorn of its medical associations. It has a biblical ring of affliction and degradation. It suggests uncontainable illness and decay of the entire body politic itself—illness it might be impossible to protect oneself against. It’s one thing if a larcenous politician sticks his hand in your pocket and grabs your wallet—that’s unpleasant enough. But what’s a great deal more unpleasant than the actual loss is the sensation of loss—the sensation that you’ve been duped, that you’ve been victimized, that you’ve failed to protect something—and the very intense subsequent sensations of helplessness and shame (symptoms of a corrupted state) have been intensified exponentially, as we learn, daily, over and over, what’s being done to the environment in the name of profits, what’s being done to the ideal of a nation of laws in the service of personal gain—and, especially, what’s being done to individuals, to families, to children, by means of kidnapping, illegal incarceration, illegal deportation, and flat-out disappearings, in illustration of the will and ability of those holding the reins to exercise unconstrained and capricious power.

While so many of us have been paralyzed in the face of these assaults on our rights, our well-being, our neighbors, there have been others who have acted in defiance, who have spoken out loudly. A number of journalists have continued to record abominations. Our hopes have hung on the courage of those who resist, some of whom, as we know, have paid the ultimate price. The newly elected have been elected largely to listen to the voices of those courageous people, and follow their lead in protecting the interests of everyone. It’s for them now to show courage and to justify our provisional faith in them. The roles are clear. The new lawmakers have been charged with preparing for a sustainable republic that represents the whole variety of people who live in our country and people who come to it with hope. And we, their constituents, must keep insisting that they do. Whether we succeed or fail to rectify the unspeakable mess we’re in, we succeed or fail together.

entries.title: Red, White, Green, Yellow, and Blue
entries.summary: On September 7, 2025, supporters of Jair Bolsonaro marked Brazil’s Independence Day by carrying a giant American flag—“the size of a basketball court,” the New York Times journalist Jack Nicas noted with astonishment—down Avenida Paulista in São Paulo. The former president was then under trial for an attempted coup d’état that included a plot to […]
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
On September 7, 2025, supporters of Jair Bolsonaro marked Brazil’s Independence Day by carrying a giant American flag—“the size of a basketball court,” the New York Times journalist Jack Nicas noted with astonishment—down Avenida Paulista in São Paulo. The former president was then under trial for an attempted coup d’état that included a plot to assassinate President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (known as Lula), Vice President Geraldo Alckmin, and the federal Supreme Court justice Alexandre de Moraes. (The conspiracy even had a name—“Green and Yellow Dagger”—and a written plan printed at the Palácio do Planalto by a senior member of the administration.) Donald Trump had lately come to Bolsonaro’s defense, and the protesters waving the US flag that day were showing their appreciation. They called themselves “patriots.”

It was a curious choice of word. Just a month earlier, citing what he called the “witch hunt” against Bolsonaro and falsely insinuating that the US was suffering losses in its trade relationship with Brazil, Trump had imposed a 50 percent tariff on Brazilian goods. The new levies were poised to harm the country’s economy, and Brazilian exports indeed contracted right after they went into effect.

But for some far-right Brazilians, the backlash prompted by the tariffs did little to dim their support for Trump. For months Paulo Figueiredo, grandson of Brazil’s last dictator, and Jair’s son Eduardo Bolsonaro had been pressuring the US to protect Jair from imminent arrest by punishing Brazilian Supreme Court justices for prosecuting him. Alongside the tariffs, Trump invoked the Global Magnitsky Act to sanction Justice Moraes, who was presiding over Bolsonaro’s trial. Yet neither the economic offensive nor the sanctions achieved their goal. The former president was convicted and imprisoned along with high-ranking military figures involved in the plot, and the effects of the tariffs were limited: exports to the US accounted for less than 2 percent of Brazil’s GDP, and the losses were soon outweighed by an increase in soy exports to China.

That disappointing outcome did not prevent the “patriots” from continuing to appeal to the United States. Indeed their rhetoric grew still more sinister. In 2026, during a major demonstration backing Senator Flávio Bolsonaro—Jair’s eldest son—in his effort to unseat Lula in this fall’s Brazilian general elections, a group of protesters displayed a white, inflatable missile bearing the words TRUMP NUKE BRAZIL.

That slogan distilled a worldview that has spread across Brazil’s right since Trump’s return to power. America is a nation that has “made it”: strong, sovereign, generous to those who work hard, and, under Trump, devoted to God, family, and guns, with communism as its sworn enemy. Such a country is to be revered, copied, and saluted. Bolsonaro himself, a retired captain of the Brazilian army, saluted the American flag twice: in October 2017, as a presidential candidate addressing supporters in Deerfield Beach, Florida, amid chants of “USA! USA!”; and in May 2019, as president, at a business luncheon in Dallas, where he also reworked his campaign slogan into “Brazil and the United States above everything.” Anyone who stands in Trump’s way, Brazil included, risks being “nuked” or seized like Nicolás Maduro. In August the Republican congressman Carlos Gimenez posted a doctored image of Lula in the place of the captured Venezuelan leader, captioned “what awaits him.” Eduardo Bolsonaro promptly reposted it. How did the Brazilian far right end up wanting to submit to the US so completely?

Ten years earlier, on October 22, 2016, the third edition of the Liberty and Democracy Forum, a conference dedicated to free-market ideas, took place in São Paulo. The first panel, titled “The Role of the State in the Twenty-First Century,” featured Fábio Ostermann, a cofounder of the Free Brazil Movement (MBL), Senator Ana Amélia Lemos, and Jair Bolsonaro, at the time a federal deputy representing Rio de Janeiro. The discussion was moderated by Hélio Beltrão, president of the Mises Institute Brazil.

At the time I was working on my doctoral thesis on the emergence of a “new right” in Brazil, and I attended the event accompanied by one of my primary informants, Bernardo Santoro. As director of the free-market Liberal Institute, Santoro had been actively involved in Flávio Bolsonaro’s unsuccessful campaign for mayor of Rio de Janeiro, a race that had concluded just weeks earlier. When we got to the venue Ostermann, whom I had interviewed before, spotted us and confronted Santoro about the politics of Ostermann’s co-panelist. How, he asked, could a free-market advocate like Santoro support a dictator like Bolsonaro?1

At the time it was common for young libertarians to feel a strong aversion toward Jair Bolsonaro. After all, the twenty-year military dictatorship (1964–1985) under which he served as an officer was statist and authoritarian (with the exception of the first three years, when the economically liberal Castelo Branco was president)—a regime that would horrify any remotely consistent libertarian. Bolsonaro took that authoritarian, reactionary politics even further: in 1999, while serving as a federal deputy, he advocated on television for the closure of Congress and the killing of “some 30,000 people, starting with Fernando Henrique Cardoso,” the country’s president at the time. In 2011 he stated that he would rather his son die in an accident than come out as gay; three years later he argued that men should earn more than women because they do not get pregnant.

Advertisement

In 2016 Brazilian free-market campaigners were still embarrassed to be associated with the right, precisely because of the legacy of the military dictatorship. Santoro himself did not identify as a right-winger; in his view, for Brazil’s libertarians to ally with conservative—or even reactionary—politicians like Jair Bolsonaro was a tactical move rather than a gesture of deep ideological affinity. A radical program of privatization and economic liberalization was, after all, unpopular in the country, whereas Bolsonaro’s brand of right-wing thought—which railed against “gender ideology” and a so-called “gay kit” supposedly handed out to children in public schools—was winning a growing grassroots following among voters who saw Lula’s Workers’ Party (PT) as corrupt, morally depraved, and committed to rewarding idleness rather than hard work. Repeatedly in our conversations Santoro emphasized that conservatism was the means; free-market liberalism was the end.

The benefits of this alliance were mutual. It was Bolsonaro’s decision to take direction from the economist Paulo Guedes that made him palatable to Brazil’s financial elites. A highly regarded economist in libertarian circles who had emerged from among the cohort of “Chicago Boys” in the 1970s and later became Bolsonaro’s minister of the economy, Guedes worked diligently between 2017 and 2018 to assure concerned Brazilian financial elites that Bolsonaro had “become a different animal.” The candidate, he argued, had accepted the rules of the democratic game and an economic agenda centered on liberalization, as the journalist Malu Gaspar noted in the Brazilian monthly piauí. Yet it did not take long, as Gaspar also pointed out, for Guedes to get swallowed up by the very creature he had promised to “tame.”

For some time I hesitated to label Bolsonaro’s political movement fascism. Scholars have long debated whether the word technically applies to the Brazilian military regime from which his political convictions emerged. In 1969 the dependency theorist Theotonio dos Santos called the dictatorship a form of “dependent fascism,” by which he meant that it was a fascism with no national project it could actually carry out, because the regimes that promoted it were structurally subordinate to the very foreign interests—multinational capital and imperial powers—that in theory it should have opposed. The nationalist Hélio Jaguaribe, meanwhile, called it “colonial fascism,” arguing that the dictatorship had stifled any authentic nationalism and kept Brazil a virtual colony. But intellectuals such as Juan Linz, Guillermo O’Donnell, Fernando Henrique Cardoso, and Atilio Borón argued that several aspects of the dictatorship made the parallel with European fascism misleading in the first place.

Historical fascism mobilized the masses through a “party-movement.” The Brazilian dictatorship, by contrast, did the opposite: it demobilized and excluded popular sectors. It was the military establishment, not a political party, that held power, allowing only a “permitted” opposition that served as a democratic veneer for the regime.

Nor did the regime have charismatic leaders; generals took turns in office. João Figueiredo, Brazil’s last dictator, once declared that he preferred “the smell of horses” to “the smell of the people.” Though there was a movement of far-right Brazilian thinkers, known as “integralists,” who explicitly attached themselves to historical fascism, they and their primary leader, Plínio Salgado, were merely junior partners to the regime. For this reason most scholars of the Brazilian military dictatorship define it as a form of authoritarianism rooted in repression, devoid of any mass movement that would make it a style of fascism.

As Bolsonaro rose to power, it was precisely this element—the support of the masses—that his administration gained. His most energetic backing came from conservative evangelical pastors, self-employed workers, and aspiring entrepreneurs. As the anthropologist Rosana Pinheiro-Machado describes, these segments have come to form a new aspirational class, driven by anger toward a state they consider not just corrupt but blind to their interests and indifferent to their fate. A newly decentralized and Internet-powered mass party also emerged—what Marcos Nobre and researchers at the Brazilian Center of Analysis and Planning (CEBRAP) have called the “Bolsonarista Digital Party.” The far-right legislators Nikolas Ferreira and Cleitinho, with their millions of followers, represent this entity in its purest form: a network of digital-native politicians who use their fame and platforms to command loyalty, effectively parasitizing traditional parties. This year Ferreira was reelected to Congress with more than three million votes, the largest tally for a federal deputy in Brazil’s history, while Cleitinho, a senator, was elected governor of Minas Gerais in the first round.

And yet Bolsonaro’s government lacked the repressive apparatus of the military dictatorship. Like the military regime, it singled out the Supreme Court for attack—Bolsonaro hurled insults at justices and declared in 2021 that he would no longer comply with their decisions—and questioned the validity of electronic voting machines in rhetoric that echoed the dictatorship’s manipulation of electoral rules. Naturally it also needed a reincarnated “communist” enemy, which it found in the PT, the powerful left party established in 1980, toward the end of the dictatorship. But Bolsonaro’s presidency stopped short of using state power to detain, imprison, and murder its enemies en masse. Instead violence spread in a diffuse manner: access to firearms, for instance, was expanded under the guise of allowing “upstanding citizens” to defend themselves.

The military dictatorship, in other words, featured repression without mass mobilization, whereas Bolsonaro’s rule involved mass mobilization without a state-run repressive apparatus. It did, however, galvanize a persistent movement that aligned with the historian Robert Paxton’s view of fascism as a process that unfolds in stages, from the founding of an organized political formation to its rooting in political life, its alliance with conservative elites, and, sometimes, the conquest of the state. Most fascist movements, like the Ku Klux Klan, never got that far but were no less fascist for it. Yet what form of Brazilian fascism could include waving an American flag the size of a basketball court, or calling for a nuclear strike against one’s own nation?

To understand this strange development, it may seem natural to return to the theories of “dependent” and “colonial” fascism developed in the late 1960s by thinkers such as Dos Santos and Jaguaribe. Both theorists described a structural, imposed domination: Brazil, they argued, was forced to depend on a world capitalist system with its center in the United States. Under the dictatorship, that dependence was real. When the Federal Reserve sent interest rates soaring in 1979, Brazil’s debts soon became unpayable, forcing the country into the arms of the IMF and ushering in a “lost decade” of stagnation and hyperinflation. Yet this dependence on Washington was mediated by creditors and the IMF rather than openly embraced.

Today the picture is different. Brazil may indeed occupy a subordinate economic position within the international system, but that position is quite clearly not the one of dependency to which it was consigned decades ago. The limited impact of Trump’s 50 percent tariff on Brazilian goods showed how autonomous the country’s economic position has become. Brazil holds more than $300 billion in reserves, and it has much of what the world wants, from rare earths to clean energy—resources that it can leverage in negotiations with a variety of nations, rather than remaining beholden to the US. China has been its largest trading partner since 2009. None of this stopped Flávio Bolsonaro, at the Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC) in Texas this past March, from offering his country up anyway: “Brazil is America’s solution,” he declared, “to break independence on China for critical minerals, especially rare-earth elements.”

A more persuasive explanation for such rhetoric can be found in an interview that the military general and former UN peacekeeping commander Santos Cruz, who served briefly as a minister in Bolsonaro’s administration, gave last month to the journalist Bruno Torturra. At a certain point the exchange turned to how Bolsonaro’s allies had cheered Trump’s tariffs and urged Washington to punish Brazil’s Supreme Court justices. “Seeking external support, in the way it was done, is absurd,” Cruz said.

It is, in fact, an assault on Brazil’s sovereignty…. It is voluntary submission. Seeking outside interference is treason…. I consider myself a man of the right; but what this is—this isn’t “the right.” This is nothing more than a swindle.

Instead of “dependency fascism,” we might say that the contemporary Brazilian right is under the influence of “submission fascism.” Here dependence on a more powerful foreign country is not an inescapable structural condition but a “voluntary” object of desire, deliberately sought for the sake of defeating an internal enemy. In Brazil, those who beseech the US to undermine the country’s institutions and Lula’s government hope it will help them finally defeat the PT, free Jair Bolsonaro, and clear his way back to power. This choice to submit originates not just from the elites—as Jaguaribe once suggested—but also from a popular base. It is a choice made during a time of peace and democracy, rather than under the duress of war or the threat of imminent attack.

At first this desire for submission was directed toward an internal protector. In 2022 the so-called “patriots” sought to have the armed forces intervene via a coup d’état to “save” Brazil from another Workers’ Party administration, which they characterized as a “left-wing dictatorship.” As the sociologist Jonas Medeiros has described, for months they camped out near military barracks, carrying signs and chanting with religious fervor: “Armed Forces, save Brazil!” When the military failed to heed their call, the “patriots” took matters into their own hands, culminating in the ransacking of the seats of the three branches of government on January 8, 2023.

Immediately following Trump’s reelection, the imagery of salvation shifted. In 2025 signs held by “patriots” at protests read “SOS Trump” and “Help me.” The desire remained for a “moderating power” that could ensure the nation’s salvation; what changed was who would provide that salvation, and how.

If the traditional right, as represented by figures like Santos Cruz, was aghast at the prospect of treating Trump as Brazil’s savior, the response from the “new right” was more muted. Libertarians like Santoro and Guedes may have begun supporting Bolsonaro as a tactic to advance a free-market agenda, but now they have little of substance to say about his movement’s open submission to Trump, which flies in the face of their stated principles. From a neoliberal point of view, as Santoro himself has implied, it makes no sense for Brazil to commit its rare earths to the US instead of selling them to the highest bidder. Why haven’t they put up a fight?

The answer to that question lies elsewhere in the content of the economic thought they promoted. By importing radical libertarian ideas, the Brazilian new right also imported a view of the international system that was designed to curtail the economic sovereignty of peripheral nations like Brazil. As Quinn Slobodian has argued, free-market ideologues like Ludwig von Mises were willing to accept the political independence of former colonies and peripheral countries—but not their right to control their own resources or nationalize companies.2 The rights of capital were always to be prioritized over the rights of workers in the periphery. These peripheral nations could be “free,” provided they did not use that freedom to challenge foreign capital. When Trump abandoned free-market neoliberalism in favor of an “America First” agenda characterized by heavy tariffs, sanctions, and disputes over rare-earth minerals, the new right and its peripheral-nation libertarians found themselves without the vocabulary to defend their own national interests.

Renan Santos, a leader of the Free Brazil Movement, was one of the few to recognize this danger. As a presidential candidate in the 2026 elections, he openly criticized the Bolsonarista movement’s subservience to Trump and proposed pivoting instead toward a right-wing developmentalist nationalism. Brazil, in his view, ought to treat its rare earths as leverage rather than as a gift, suspending deals until the minerals could be processed at home, and bargaining hard with Washington, Tokyo, and Europe for technology and investment. Trump, he said, “only knows how to deal with people who negotiate hard with him.”

These dynamics loomed large over the election earlier this fall. Voters I interviewed during the campaign who intended to cast their ballots for Flávio Bolsonaro followed the “patriots” in choosing to submit to the US, but on somewhat different grounds. Only by joining the “shield of the Americas,” they argued, could Brazil finally put a stop to urban crime and rein in its criminal factions.

Among the elites, Flávio Bolsonaro’s most enthusiastic backers were the cattle ranchers and soybean growers of the Green and Yellow Brazil Movement. The anthropologist Caio Pompeia identifies this movement with the most politically extreme wing of Brazilian agribusiness—what he calls “agri-Bolsonaristas.”3 Its leaders dispute climate science, have called for abolishing the Environment Ministry and weakening the Forest Code, and want Indigenous lands opened to farming. They have some reason to be wary of Trump, but his second-term trade wars have so far done them more good than ill: largely unaffected by the US’s aggressive tariff hikes on Brazil’s own goods, they profited handsomely when China replaced American soy with Brazilian soy. Seeking high-risk, short-term economic gains, they demand the freedom to clear-cut forests and encroach upon protected or demarcated lands in the Amazon and other biomes.

As for the financial elites, they would have preferred São Paulo Governor Tarcísio de Freitas; they supported Flávio Bolsonaro only because they had no other choice. To appease them, after finishing the first round of the election ahead of Lula, with a lead of more than two million votes, Flávio openly proposed an economic program inspired by that of Javier Milei, much to the delight of the fringe libertarians. But as Santoro warned in 2016, libertarianism is inherently unpopular among much of the electorate. Flávio’s choice to loudly and clearly announce his intended economic agenda—including cutting around 250 billion reais (more than $44 billion) from public spending and requiring “free” negotiation between employers and employees—surely contributed to his loss in the election’s second round.

The first-round votes, which delivered a majority to pro-Bolsonaro senators and raised the prospect of gaining control over the Supreme Federal Court, also emboldened Flávio. Soon he started openly stating that he wished to amend the Constitution in order to “re-democratize the country,” a claim that many voters interpreted—correctly—as a sign that he would have both the legislative and the judicial branches in his pocket. A number of Brazilians who until then had been undecided or had abstained in the first round were gripped by panic. In one interview I conducted during the campaign, a voter gave voice to this shared understanding that a Flávio administration would dismantle social and labor rights:

What’s going to happen is that they’ll impose a dictatorship in Brazil, with only his family in power. The Senate is his; everyone there is already on his side. Flávio has carte blanche to do whatever he wants—and impeachment is off the table; with this Senate, it’s just not possible. And this whole idea of ​​hourly wages and negotiating directly with one’s boss—it’s going to be a pro-business government.

In just three weeks, Lula gained over 10 million new votes, ultimately winning by a margin of 4.4 million. As the sociologist Thais Pavez remarked to me, invoking Walter Benjamin, the majority of Brazilians pulled the emergency brake just in time.

But the train has not yet come to a complete stop; the “America First, Brazil Last” project remains alive. Three days after the election Flávio Bolsonaro fled to the US and released a letter declaring himself the true president of Brazil. Soon afterward, I interviewed voters who had backed Lula only in the runoff out of fear. The women spoke of suspicion. “Trump gave him political shelter,” one told me. “I don’t rule out that he’s planning something with Flávio. I saw that one of his aides helped Flávio escape. It makes you wary.” The men, without being prompted, spoke of sovereignty. “If Flávio had won, he would have handed the rare earths to Trump,” one said. “Brazil would have become America’s backyard.”

entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
The sixth episode of Endgame with Fintan O’Toole was taped live, with a remote audience, a week after the midterms dealt a resounding rebuke to the Trump administration and a huge congressional victory to the Democrats. Rhodes and Taylor offer their interpretations of the election results and talk about what the Democrats in Congress will need to do in order to avoid squandering this historic opportunity: govern as populists and pass legislation supported by a great majority of Americans, like ending the war in Iran, regulating AI and data center construction, and organizing around Medicare for All.

Ben Rhodes is a writer and the cochair of National Security Action, an advocacy group based in Washington, D.C. He was the Deputy National Security Adviser for Strategic Communications and Speechwriting under President Obama from 2009 to 2017 and has been contributing to The New York Review since 2023. His latest book, All We Say: The Battle for American Identity, was published earlier this year.

Astra Taylor is a documentary filmmaker, political organizer, and writer who has contributed to the Review since 2020. Her latest film is What Is Democracy? (2018) and her latest book, End Times Fascism and the Fight for the Living World,was cowritten with Naomi Klein and published earlier this year.
